'''Ludwig Berwald''' (8 December 1883 &ndash; 20 April 1942) was a German [[mathematician]] best known for his contributions to [[differential geometry]], especially [[finsler manifold|Finsler geometry]]. He taught at the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]] and the [[German University in Prague]] for 32 years, publishing 54 papers, before being deported by the Nazi [[Schutzstaffel|SS]] to the [[Łódź Ghetto|Łódź Jewish Ghetto]], where he and his wife Hedwig died within a year.<ref name="mt" />

==Biography==
Ludwig was one of three children of Max Berwald, an East Prussian owner of a famous bookstore, and Friedericke Fischel. They were "[[Jewish]] with Max coming from [[East Prussia]] and his wife being a native of [[Prague]]."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www-history.mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Berwald.html |work=st-andrews.ac.uk |title=Ludwig Berwald }}</ref> In 1900, the family moved to Munich, where Ludwig matriculated at the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]] in 1902.<ref name="mt">{{MacTutor Biography|id= Berwald}}</ref> There he studied mathematics under [[Aurel Voss]], alongside notable mathematicians [[Hugo Dingler]] and [[Fritz Noether]],<ref name="mathgen">{{cite web|title=Aurel Voss|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=49178|website=Mathematics Genealogy Project|accessdate=8 July 2016}}</ref> and received his PhD in 1908 for his thesis entitled ''Über die Krümmungseigenschaften der Brennflächen eines geradlinigen Strahlsystems und der in ihm enthaltenen Regelflächen'' (''On the properties of curvature on the internal surfaces of rectilinear systems, and surfaces contained therein'').<ref name="NGB">{{cite book|last1=Sweet|first1=William|title=New German Biography|date=1955|page=173|edition=2|url=https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/gnd13554548X.html#ndbcontent|accessdate=8 July 2016}}</ref> Due to sanatorium treatment for pulmonary illness, he was unable to continue his work in Munich. Through friends, he eventually became a lecturer at the [[German University in Prague]], achieving full professorship in 1924. There, he developed friendships and successful collaborations with fellow mathematicians [[Georg Pick]], [[Paul Funk]], and [[Élie Cartan]], publishing some 54 articles<ref name="mt" /> which significantly advanced the field of Finsler geometry, pioneering important concepts which still bear his name such as Berwald curvature, Berwald spray,<ref>{{cite web|last1=Shen|first1=Zhongmin|title=Lecture Notes on Finsler Geometry|url=http://www.math.iupui.edu/~zshen/Research/papers/lecture/lecture.html|website=www.math.iupui.edu|accessdate=8 July 2016}}</ref> and the Berwald–Moór metric function.<ref name="ShenBook">{{cite book|last1=Shen|first1=Zhongmin|title=Differential Geometry of Spray and Finsler Spaces|date=2001|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=9789401597272|page=27|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wIHrCAAAQBAJ|language=en}}</ref> For extending the concept of Riemann curvature to Finsler spaces, Berwald has been credited as the founder of differential geometry of Finsler spaces.<ref>Shen 2001, p. 1</ref> On 22 October 1941, the day after submitting his last article,<ref name=Pinl/> the sickly 57-year-old Berwald was deported to the [[Łódź Ghetto]] in Poland in the third transportation of Jews by the German secret police. The Berwalds were two of 55 people who lived in 48 Maryśinska Street in a one-room approximately {{convert|20|x|20|ft|m|0}} with no beds. Hedwig, eight years older than her husband, died 27 March 1942; Ludwig followed 23 days later.<ref name="Pinl">{{cite journal|last1=Pinl|first1=Max|title=In Memory of Ludwig Berwald|journal=Scripta Mathematica|date=1964|volume=27|issue=3|pages=193–203|url=http://titurel.org/MathApprObit/BerwaldPinl.pdf|accessdate=8 July 2016}}</ref><ref> Clary, David C. (2024). [https://doi.org/10.1142/q0436 ''The Lost Scientists of World War II.''] World Scientific Publishing, ISBN 9781800614918. </ref>
